item.title: Election 2026: Tiburon Town Council hopefuls talk traffic, finances, housing at Ark forum
item.description: Tiburon Town Council candidates mostly agreed at a Sept. 29 forum that residents should help oversee town finances but split on Flock cameras, housing sites and park funding.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon Town Council candidates mostly agreed at a Sept. 29 forum that residents should help oversee town finances but split on Flock cameras, housing sites and paying for parks.

More than 50 people packed Town Hall’s council chambers and nearly 150 people tuned in on The Ark’s Instagram page for the forum, hosted by The Ark and moderated by the League of Women Voters of Marin County, to hear from incumbents Alice Fredericks and Jack Ryan and challengers Kathleen Defever, Chuck Hornbrook and Faris Jafar. The top three vote-getters in the Nov. 3 election will win four-year terms that end November 2030.

Defever, 48, is a lawyer who has served since 2018 on the Planning Commission and is seeking her first term on the council.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

In her opening statement, she pointed to her expertise in insurance and her work representing fire victims, saying the denser housing the town must plan for under its housing element, which requires sites for 639 units by 2031, would add to fire risk on the peninsula.

“I am the person most equipped to handle those questions and to come up with constructive solutions,” Defever said.

Fredericks, 86, is a former behavioral-medicine researcher at the University of California at San Francisco who is the longest-serving councilmember in Tiburon’s history and has served as mayor on five occasions. She’s seeking a seventh term after being first elected in 2001.

She pointed to her work representing the town on countywide agencies, such as the Transportation Authority of Marin, and on county sea-level-rise planning committees.

“My work in the last few years has focused on community and government bodies that foster collaboration and coordination — and please don’t go to sleep, because in this day and age, it’s very important,” Fredericks said.

She also said the town is not done with park improvements, floating the idea of acquiring the Richardson Bay Sanitary District’s remaining land for a community center.

Hornbrook, 59, is a part-time adviser to clean-energy companies and a member of the Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission.

item.title: Tiburon sanitary district considers overhaul of odor-control system
item.description: Sanitary District No. 5 of Marin is weighing $1 million to $11 million fixes for the 21-year-old odor-control system at its Paradise Drive plant in Tiburon.
item.content:encoded:
Jim Miller said his Centro West Street home might have the best view in town, if not the world. This year, he said, it has also come with the smell of the sewage plant on Paradise Drive.

Sanitary District No. 5 of Marin, which runs the plant, is weighing what to do about the 21-year-old system meant to contain the odor. Its choices run from $1 million to $2 million to rehabilitate the equipment to roughly $11 million over 20 years to replace it.

The district’s board voted unanimously Sept. 17 to accept the Carollo Engineers report laying out the options and directed District Manager Tony Rubio to work with the district’s capital improvement program committee on budgeting and implementation. Rubio’s staff report recommended that the work focus on rehabilitating the current system. No project, budget or construction timeline has been approved.

“We’ve got an odor-control system that works, but with any big project, you have to prioritize funding — how much and how fast,” Rubio said. “It goes back to committee for figuring out all those loose ends.”

item.title: Election 2026: Tamalpais Union board hopefuls split over trust, budget at forum
item.description: Seven candidates for three Tamalpais Union High School District board seats split over whether the board has lost community trust, at a Sept. 28 forum in Larkspur.
item.content:encoded:
Two incumbents and five challengers vying for three Tamalpais Union High School District board seats are divided over whether the board has lost the community’s trust after a year of contested votes on support programs for Black students, cellphones and the district’s alternative schools.

Six of the seven candidates made their cases Sept. 28 at a League of Women Voters of Marin County forum at the Kreps Conference Center in Larkspur, co-hosted by Marin Promise Partnership. Challenger Maria Sandoval, a Mill Valley resident who teaches Spanish at a San Francisco private school and serves on the Marin County Free Library Commission, did not attend. In her League of Women Voters guide answers, she listed rebuilding trust through listening and collaboration as her first priority.

The district runs Redwood High School, the main public high school for Tiburon and Belvedere students, and Tamalpais High School, which serves Strawberry, along with Archie Williams High School in San Anselmo and two alternative schools. Board members are elected districtwide.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

The two incumbents on the ballot, board President Cynthia Roenisch and Kevin Saavedra, cast the race as a question of experience, arguing the district has steadied its finances and raised test scores under Superintendent Courtney Goode and needs seasoned board members through a tightening budget. Most of the challengers said the board must first rebuild trust with students, parents and teachers.

The third seat is open because board member Emily Uhlhorn chose not to seek reelection. She will finish her term and become executive director of the Tam High Foundation in January.

Roenisch, a Corte Madera resident who teaches Advanced Placement English at Alameda High School and is a former litigator, served on the Kentfield School District board before joining the Tam board and led the search that hired Goode. Saavedra, of San Anselmo, described his background as private equity and investment banking; his two children graduated from Sir Francis Drake High, now Archie Williams. He is the only candidate who did not file a statement for the county voter guide.

The moderator, reading from questions submitted by the public, prefaced one by citing “significant discord between the district and the community,” evidenced by contentious board meetings.

item.title: Election 2026: Open governor’s race, billionaire tax top California ballot
item.description: Peninsula ballots carry an open California governor’s race, 14 state propositions including a one-time billionaire tax, and an open Assembly seat.
item.content:encoded:
Ballots arriving in peninsula mailboxes this week carry an open governor’s race, 14 statewide propositions — among them a one-time 5% tax on billionaires and two competing measures that would cancel it — and an Assembly seat that two Democrats are vying to fill.

Marin County elections officials began mailing ballots to every active registered voter by Oct. 5. The last day to register is Oct. 19, though voters can still register and vote at a vote center or the county elections office through Election Day, Nov. 3, when polls are open 7 a.m.-8 p.m.

The Ark has covered the local races and measures on peninsula ballots in separate stories. This roundup covers the state and federal contests: the offices first, then the propositions. Each of the 14 propositions needs a simple majority to pass.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Governor: Becerra vs. Hilton

State official, all voters

Gov. Gavin Newsom is termed out, and the race to succeed him pits Democrat Xavier Becerra, a former U.S. Health and Human Services secretary, California attorney general and longtime Los Angeles-area congressman, against Republican Steve Hilton of Atherton, a former Fox News host and onetime senior adviser to British Prime Minister David Cameron.

Becerra led the June 2 primary statewide with 28%, ahead of Hilton’s 24.6%. In Marin, Becerra ran second to Democrat Tom Steyer, who did not advance, while Hilton drew 14.2%. A Republican hasn’t won the governor’s office since 2006.

Becerra has pledged to declare a state of emergency to fund 40,000 already-approved affordable homes and to fully fund the court-ordered drug treatment created by Proposition 36, the 2024 measure that stiffened penalties for some drug and theft crimes. He would also use emergency powers to freeze utility rates and crack down on price gouging. Hilton, endorsed by President Donald Trump, would eliminate state income tax on the first $150,000 of earnings and set a flat rate above that, halve the gas tax, roll back greenhouse gas and renewable-energy mandates, ban street camping outright and repeal the state’s sanctuary law.

item.title: Reed school district inclusion efforts filmed for documentary series
item.description: A crew for Andy Garcia’s public-television docuseries filmed Reed Union School District classrooms Sept. 24 for a segment on including students with disabilities.
item.content:encoded:
A film crew for a public-television docuseries hosted by actor Andy Garcia spent Sept. 24 in Reed Union School District classrooms, recording how the district includes students with disabilities.

The segment, “Breaking Down Barriers for Neurodivergent Learners,” is set to air on “All Access with Andy Garcia,” a short-form series that runs between longer programs on public-television stations nationwide. Garcia is known for roles in “Ocean’s Eleven” and “The Godfather Part III.”

Documentarians filmed interviews with district officials inside an unused Del Mar Middle School classroom and captured classroom footage there as well as at Reed and Bel Aire elementary schools. The segment is scheduled for release before the end of the year.

The district board approved the filming agreement without discussion Sept. 15. It barred filming any student in an identifiable way without a parent’s signed consent, cost the district nothing and gives the district a chance to review footage of its students and staff before broadcast.

item.media:description: Del Mar Middle School Principal Chad Stuart (left) and Sam Drazin, executive director of the nonprofit Changing Perspectives, are filmed walking and talking on Sept. 24 at the school for ‘All Access with Andy Garcia,’ a public-television series. Drazin says the Reed district is a model of how schools can put the nonprofit’s work into practice. (Francisco Martinez / The Ark)

item.title: Belvedere plans standalone fix for Hawthorne Lane stairs
item.description: Belvedere wants to rebuild the worn stairs at the top of Hawthorne Lane with a railed platform and bench now, ahead of any broader makeover of Centennial Park.
item.content:encoded:
The wooden stairs at the top of Belvedere’s Hawthorne Lane lead walkers straight into Bella Vista Avenue, and the city wants to rebuild them now rather than wait for a broader makeover of Centennial Park below.

Public Works Director Antony Boyd told the Parks, Open Spaces and Lanes Committee Sept. 17 that the city’s maintenance supervisor had raised concerns about the stairs’ condition. Boyd proposed refining an existing conceptual design, getting contractor quotes and handling the stairs as a standalone project.

Under that design people climbing the lane would step onto a wooden platform before reaching the street. The platform would have railings and room for a bench overlooking Centennial Park, and it would sit largely within the existing footprint, on a bare-earth landing.

Boyd said the change would improve pedestrian safety. Committee Vice Chair Nicholas Markman noted that the deck would also line up with stairs across the street, helping connect the two sections of the lane.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: A new wooden bench sits atop an existing concrete bench on Belvedere’s Park Lane, which connects Golden Gate and Belvedere avenues. City staff reported the bench finished the week of the Sept. 17 Parks, Open Spaces and Lanes Committee meeting. The lane’s handrails are still awaiting paint. The committee is weighing a similar landing with a bench to replace deteriorating stairs at the top of Hawthorne Lane. (Ted McDonnell / For The Ark)

item.title: Belvedere-Tiburon Library board says more time is needed for facilities plan
item.description: The Belvedere-Tiburon Library Agency board heard its first long-term facilities plan Sept. 21 but held off adopting it over concerns it mixed maintenance with new projects.
item.content:encoded:
Automatic doors, a redesigned service desk, more electric-vehicle chargers and a $1.45 million solar system are among the potential projects in the Belvedere-Tiburon Library’s first long-term facilities plan.

The Belvedere-Tiburon Library Agency board heard the plan Sept. 21 but did not formally adopt it after members expressed concerns that the draft was combining several separate aspects.

The sticking point was a makerspace assessment, which the plan lists among projects to take up within two years. Board member Anthony Hooker said the plan appeared to be “mixing a couple of things together.”

“That has nothing to do with maintenance and capital improvement,” Hooker said, a sentiment board Vice Chair Roxanne Richards supported.

item.title: Crib Notes: Waterfront mansion in Belvedere hits the market for $32 million
item.description: A newly completed three-level waterfront home at 46 Cliff Road on Belvedere Island, descending to the edge of Richardson Bay, is on the market for $32 million.
item.content:encoded:
A newly completed waterfront mansion descending from a private Belvedere road to the edge of Richardson Bay has hit the market for $32 million.

The three-level home at 46 Cliff Road has 5,099 square feet of interior space on a roughly 0.38-acre lot, according to the listing. The property includes four en suite bedrooms, five full bathrooms, 1,360 square feet of terraces and a junior accessory dwelling unit with a private waterfront deck.

Listing agent Tania Toubba of Sotheby’s International Realty said the property had been on the market since mid-September and had already drawn broker tours, private showings and visitors to an unusual public open house.

The house was offered at $29.5 million in March 2025, The Ark reported at the time.

item.title: Picks of the Week: Belvedere Home Made Film Festival returns; Tiburon Native American celebration
item.description: The Belvedere Home Made Film Festival screens 30 local shorts Oct. 9 in Belvedere Community Park, and Tiburon celebrates Native American arts Oct. 11 in Zelinsky Park.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere Home Made Film Festival returns: The third annual Belvedere Home Made Film Festival starts at 6 p.m. Oct. 9 in Belvedere Community Park with a performance by the Windsor Street Blues Band, followed by a program of 30 short films. Each film was made by locals and runs under three minutes, covering a range of interests and themes. Before the festival, Be Ready Belvedere, the city’s emergency-preparedness working group, will hold a shelter-in-place event from 5 to 6 p.m. at the park. Volunteers will hand out stay-box supplies to residents registered with AlertMarin and help others sign up. The event is free; bring low seating. bhmff.com.

Tiburon Native American celebration: Tiburon’s second annual Celebration of Native American Arts and Culture runs 1-4 p.m. Oct. 11 in Zelinsky Park. The event will feature the Sewam American Indian Dance group, led by Eddie Madril and Sara Moncada of Tiburon. The artist known as Blue will play a variety of flutes, and there will be arts vendors and food from Dramatic Events Marin’s food truck, including a bison burger. The event is hosted by the Tiburon Heritage & Arts Commission and Diversity Inclusion Task Force. The celebration comes the day before Indigenous Peoples Day, which is marked as an alternative to the federal Columbus Day holiday. The event is free. arkn.ws/NAAC.

item.title: Tiburon financier Mark Hanf pleads guilty in Pacific Private Money fraud
item.description: Tiburon resident Mark Hanf and his former chief operating officer pleaded guilty in the Pacific Private Money fraud and agreed to at least $71.8 million in restitution.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon resident Mark Hanf pleaded guilty Sept. 30 to federal fraud and money-laundering charges, admitting he deceived investors in his Novato lending firm and agreeing to repay them at least $71.8 million.

Hanf, 66, the founder and former chief executive of Pacific Private Money, entered the pleas before U.S. District Judge Jacqueline Scott Corley in San Francisco, a week after Hoai-Nam Chu Phan, 58, of Novato, the firm’s former chief operating officer, pleaded guilty Sept. 23 to the same wire-fraud conspiracy count.

Both men pleaded guilty to every count they faced, reversing the not-guilty pleas each entered Sept. 1.

Phan is set to be sentenced at 10 a.m. Feb. 10 and Hanf at 10 a.m. 17. Each faces a maximum of 20 years in prison on the conspiracy count, and Hanf 10 more on the money-laundering count, though maximum terms are rarely imposed and the judge will weigh the federal sentencing guidelines.

Victims addressed the court at both hearings, according to the court’s minutes, which do not record what they said. Corley referred both men to U.S. Probation for presentence reports. Neither man was taken into custody, the minutes show.

Among the investors is Tiburon resident Peter Siewert, 67, who said in an email that he once had more than $100,000 invested with the firm, which “performed very well,” and that his balance was about $20,000 when it filed for bankruptcy. Siewert said he was surprised and disappointed, and he expects to file a claim soon.

“I dealt only with Nam, who was a very pleasant person to deal with,” Siewert wrote, referring to Phan.

Both men admitted misleading investors

As part of their pleas Hanf and Phan admitted defrauding investors through false statements and omissions about the funds’ financial condition, their use of new investors’ money to pay earlier investors who withdrew and the safety of the investments, from December 2021 through December 2025, according to prosecutors. They admitted releasing “sanitized financial statements” that misled investors, manipulating the loan tapes — the schedules of loans a fund holds — shown to at least one investor and telling a corporate investor the firm still owned loans they knew had already been sold.

item.title: Demolition of Belvedere’s Mallard Pointe gets green light
item.description: Crews are mobilizing to demolish Belvedere’s 22 Mallard Pointe apartments after an Oct. 1 permit, but one tenant remains and a silt-curtain dispute could stall part of the work.
item.content:encoded:
This story was updated from a preliminary version posted Oct. 2.

Crews are mobilizing to tear down Belvedere’s 22 Mallard Pointe apartments after the city issued a lagoon bulkhead permit Oct. 1, which it required before demolition could begin. But one tenant remains, and a dispute over a silt curtain could stall part of the work.

Demolition can be completed safely in the next 60 days, said Bruce Dorfman, principal of developer Thompson Dorfman Partners. Bulkhead work will begin as soon as removing some of the housing and garages opens access to it, he said, and “demo and bulkhead work will be performed sequentially in segments and largely simultaneously.”

The city said in an Oct. 5 update that demolition, beginning with asbestos and other hazardous-materials removal inside the vacant buildings, is expected to start in late October or early November and run about five weeks. Bulkhead replacement could begin as early as the week of Oct. 5, depending on site access and the installation of erosion and stormwater controls, the city said.

Under the project’s demolition approval, bulkhead replacement must begin within 14 calendar days after demolition starts, but nothing requires demolition to go first, the city said.

Debris will be trucked to Redwood Landfill in Novato by one of two routes the city posted Sept. 30, along Beach Road or San Rafael Avenue.

In the meantime, firefighters from the Tiburon and Southern Marin fire protection districts and the Marin County Fire Department are holding training exercises at the complex through Oct. 12, practicing forcible entry, searches and ventilation without live fire.

Demolition can begin once the developer gives the city details on capping all of the site’s utilities except those serving the duplex containing apartment units 3 and 4, said Rebecca Markwick, Belvedere’s director of planning and building. Dorfman confirmed that one tenant is still living at Mallard Pointe past the end of the notice period. Every other tenant has relocated.

Tenants received 180-day notices to vacate Feb. 6 and, as the law requires, 60-day notices July 15, he said. That was the day the demolition permit was issued. The 60-day notices expired Sept. 14.

“We’re following the appropriate legal process, and out of respect for this individual, we cannot comment further,” Dorfman said.

item.title: Three fire agencies drill at Belvedere's Mallard Pointe complex through Oct. 12
item.description: Firefighters from Tiburon Fire, Southern Marin Fire and Marin County Fire are training at the Mallard Pointe apartments through Oct. 12 before demolition.
item.content:encoded:
Firefighters from the Tiburon Fire Protection District, the Southern Marin Fire Protection District and the Marin County Fire Department are training at the Mallard Pointe apartments in Belvedere through Oct. 12 before the complex is demolished.

Crews are simulating a full first-alarm response to a structure fire at the 1-22 Mallard Road site, with about 15 firefighters at each session, said Travis Terrell, the Tiburon district’s A-shift training battalion chief.

The drills include hose deployment, victim searches, interior fire attack and vertical ventilation — cutting openings in roofs to release heat and smoke. Fog machines stand in for smoke, and no live fire is used.

Training generally runs 9 a.m.-5 p.m., depending on call volume, with most drills ending earlier, Terrell said. The developer has fenced the site, so there is no public access.

Neighbors may see more fire engines and firefighters in the area, and the activity is not an emergency, the city said. Noise will be well below that of the daily construction nearby, Terrell said.

The developer gave the district a short window to train before Pacific Gas and Electric Co. shuts off the complex’s electric and gas service, he said.

“Access to structures for multiagency training in Marin County is extremely rare, and finding locations that accommodate a full first-alarm response rather than just one or two engines is even less common,” he said.

Belvedere issued a permit Oct. 1 to replace the complex’s lagoon bulkhead, which the city required before the developer could tear down the 22 apartments to make way for 40 homes.

item.title: Election 2026: Reed schools’ Measure O seeks $115 million bond for campus repairs
item.description: Voters will decide Nov. 3 on Measure O, a $115 million bond to repair and upgrade the Reed Union School District’s three schools.
item.content:encoded:
Voters will decide Nov. 3 on Measure O, a $115 million bond to repair and upgrade the Reed Union School District’s three schools.

Measure O needs 55% approval to pass. The tax would be levied on properties in the district, which includes Tiburon, Belvedere and east Corte Madera, starting in fiscal year 2027-2028, when the district expects the rate to peak at $30 per $100,000 of assessed value. That works out to $300 a year for every $1 million of assessed value.

Two parcel taxes on the same ballot would also reach district property owners: Measure P, a 15-year countywide childcare tax of 5 cents per square foot of building, and Measure CC, a 30-year Marin Healthcare District tax of 14 cents a square foot to expand MarinHealth Medical Center’s emergency room and intensive care. Together they would cost the owner of a 2,000-square-foot house $380 a year.

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

The district estimates the rate would average $26.63 per $100,000 over the life of the bonds, with the tax collected for the last time in fiscal 2060-2061. The levy would raise about $6.2 million a year, according to the ballot question, and the district’s tax rate statement estimates that repaying the full $115 million would cost $213 million in principal and interest.

No bond money can be used for teacher or administrator salaries, and the measure requires a citizens’ oversight committee and annual independent audits. The measure’s text also says the money must be spent on the district’s schools and cannot be taken by the state or county.

Reed Union School District board President Shelby Pasarell Tsai said the bond measure was important because systems at the district’s three campuses — Reed and Bel Aire elementary schools and Del Mar Middle School — need serious work, from leaking and failing roofs to degraded clay pipes and irrigation.

“Anyone who owns a home knows after 20 years, buildings need some pretty serious maintenance,” Pasarell Tsai said.

Pasarell Tsai is the lead author of the ballot argument in favor of Measure O, which she signed with Jessica Etchevers, president of the district’s PTA; former school board member A.J. Brady; Belvedere Councilmember Jane Cooper; and Tiburon Councilmember Jack Ryan. Pasarell Tsai, Cooper and Ryan are all seeking reelection Nov. 3.

No argument against Measure O was filed with the Marin County Elections Department.

item.title: Tiburon resident, educator helps bring Native American culture to community
item.description: Tiburon’s Eddie Madril, an assistant professor at San Francisco State and founder of Sewam American Indian Dance, is co-organizing the town’s Native American celebration Oct. 11.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon resident Eddie Madril thought he was going to be an architect.

He studied calculus and physics and says he envisioned himself working on the 40th floor of a San Francisco or New York high-rise.

Madril ended up as an educator focusing on Native American culture, but he says his expertise didn’t necessarily begin with scholarly research and book reading.

“It came from just a life, over 45 years of experience being in the community, understanding and being … in the same rooms where things that were discussed on legalities, customs, traditions, ceremonies, art, dance, music — all of this stuff,” he says.

Madril is an assistant professor in San Francisco State University’s American Indian studies department and the founder of the Sewam American Indian Dance group, which has performed in the U.S. and abroad, including in 2025 at the 51st Festival of World Cultures in Gannat, France, an event that partners with UNESCO.

Madril is also a co-organizer of Tiburon’s second celebration of Native American culture and heritage, scheduled for 1-4 p.m. Oct. 11 — the day before Indigenous Peoples Day — at Zelinsky Park between Town Hall and the Belvedere-Tiburon Library.

item.title: Election 2026: Community engagement, fiscal oversight define Strawberry Recreation District race
item.description: Doug Twillman, appointed to the Strawberry Recreation District board last year, faces challenger Aliza Hawkins Nov. 3 for the district’s open two-year seat.
item.content:encoded:
The two residents who sought a vacant Strawberry Recreation District board seat last year are running for the same seat Nov. 3, this time before voters.

The board picked Doug Twillman, a finance veteran and triathlete, on a 3-1 vote in September 2025. Aliza Hawkins, a marketing professional, mother of two and certified counselor, is challenging him in a rare contested election for a district that has historically struggled to find candidates.

Twillman and Hawkins are vying for the one open two-year seat. Incumbents Peter Teese, Sohrab Saghezchi and Sarah Waterfield, along with newcomer David Morgenthaler, will compete for three open four-year seats. Board members receive $100 per regular meeting, with a maximum of $500 per month.

Election 2026: The Strawberry Recreation District two-year candidates at a glance

Election 2026: Read complete coverage at thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Established in 1949, the Strawberry Recreation District is an independent special district serving about 6,000 residents in areas of unincorporated Mill Valley and unincorporated Tiburon east of Highway 101. In addition to the rec center and headquarters on East Strawberry Drive, it maintains four parks, a public dock, several walking trails and the Water Tank Hill open space.

According to the district, it receives 3.5 cents per dollar of basic property tax paid to Marin County, roughly 15% of its annual revenue. The rest, about $3 million, comes mostly from fees for classes, facility rentals and memberships.

The district hired playground company GameTime in July under a $2.4 million contract to build a playground on grass between the tennis courts and baseball fields at Strawberry Park. A revised quote and a separate bid for a restroom pushed the total past $3 million on Sept. 8, and the board told the company to come back under its $2.5 million ceiling. The district plans to break ground in 2027.

Aliza Hawkins: Challenger wants more residents involved

Hawkins, 39, said she would focus on drawing more residents in and on inclusive programming. She describes herself as social, outgoing and deeply connected to Strawberry.

She moved to Strawberry from Southern California with her husband, James, and their two children about 2½ years ago. The family bought a home near the recreation center last year.

item.title: Election 2026: The Strawberry Recreation District two-year candidates at a glance
item.description: The Strawberry Recreation District two-year candidates at a glance
item.content:encoded:
Aliza Hawkins, challenger

Years as resident: 2½.

Occupation: Former senior account specialist at Rakuten Advertising and certified counselor.

Education: Bachelor’s degree in business administration and a master’s degree in counseling, both from The Master’s University.

Civic background: Marriage and family counselor at Lighthouse Community Church in Torrance from 2019 to 2021.

Key issues: Community engagement and inclusive programming.

Quote: “We want our kids to grow up in a community that’s not just people who have kids and people who have young kids, but really a diverse representation of ages and different stages of life.”

Doug Twillman, incumbent

Years as resident: 27.

Occupation: Financial analyst and consultant in commercial real estate.

Education: Bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering from the University of California at Davis and a master’s degree in business from the University of San Francisco.

Civic background: Appointed to the Strawberry Recreation District board in September 2025; member of San Francisco’s Olympic Club, where he chaired the investment committee from 2012 to 2014.

Key issues: Fiscal oversight and completing the new playground.

Quote: “The budget should be well understood so that we can hold the contractors accountable and the community can hold us accountable for a successful physical and fiscal outcome.”

item.title: Local stories take the screen as Belvedere Home Made Film Festival returns
item.description: About 30 short films screen at the third annual Belvedere Home Made Film Festival, which begins at 6 p.m. Oct. 9 at Belvedere Community Park.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon resident Mark Freiberg looked outside his bayside window one day in 2024 and noticed an unusual boat. There in Paradise Cay, among the other ships he watches daily, was a small towboat.

“I saw this little boat, and I’ve got to say, it’s an odd-looking boat,” Freiberg said. “I just got very curious about it.”

That curiosity grew when the boat began working near the Corinthian Yacht Club that year. Its extended stay gave Freiberg opportunities to speak with crew members and meet the boat’s owner. He also recorded some footage of the boat from the air with his drone camera.

This spring that footage became the raw material for “P Cay” — Freiberg’s short video submission to the third annual Belvedere Home Made Film Festival. The family-friendly festival will screen about 30 short films by community members, each three minutes or less, at 6 p.m. Oct. 9 at Belvedere Community Park.

The free event invites families to bring blankets and sit on the lawn to watch the show, which will also include live music by the Windsor Street Blues Band, popcorn, hot cocoa and homemade soup. The band plays at 6 p.m., and the films will start about 7. A drop-off point and limited seating will be available on Community Road for older adults and people with mobility concerns. Before the festival, Be Ready Belvedere, the city’s emergency-preparedness working group, will hold a shelter-in-place event from 5 to 6 p.m. at the park. Volunteers will hand out stay-box supplies to Belvedere residents registered with AlertMarin and help others sign up.

They are among about 30 films in the Belvedere Home Made Film Festival, which begins at 6 p.m. Oct. 9 at Belvedere Community Park. (Screengrabs from video)

item.title: Tiburon’s Cinelounge to host Bruce Dern for inaugural fundraising gala
item.description: Academy Award-nominated actor Bruce Dern will be the guest of honor Nov. 5 at the first fundraising gala for a new nonprofit supporting Tiburon movie theater Cinelounge.
item.content:encoded:
Academy Award-nominated actor Bruce Dern will be the guest of honor Nov. 5 at the first fundraising gala for a new nonprofit supporting downtown Tiburon movie theater Cinelounge.

The evening runs 5:30-9:30 p.m. at the theater and includes a reception ahead of a screening of “Dernsie: The Amazing Life of Bruce Dern,” a documentary about his life that debuted earlier this year at the Cannes Film Festival. The screening, limited to 60 people, will be followed by a conversation with Dern and “Dernsie” director Mike Mendez. Reception-only tickets are also available.

“When you have talent like this, … and they come to Tiburon, it’s a once-in-a-lifetime event,” says Christian Meoli, who owns the theater with his wife, Camilla Meoli. “And (Dern) has such an amazing track record of working in the business in films for, I mean, my God, almost, over seven decades that we also thought that he was a great fit for the demographic in Tiburon.”
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
